title: Why cells stay small
hook: A cell feeds through its skin. Grow it ten times wider: does it get more skin per inside?

knows: area and volume of a cube
cells take in food and get rid of waste
doesNotKnow: that surface-to-volume ratio falls as size rises

misconception: A cell 10 times wider has 10 times more surface per unit of inside (or at least the same).
objective: The learner can explain that surface grows with the square of width and volume with the cube, so surface per unit of volume is 6/width for a cube and a 10-times-wider cell has a tenth as much surface per unit of inside.

claims.text: A cube of width w has surface 6w^2 and volume w^3, so surface per unit of volume is 6/w: 6 at width 1 and 0.6 at width 10 (600 squares for 1,000 cubes), ten times smaller.
Food, oxygen and waste cross a cell's surface, so a larger cell has less surface to supply each bit of its inside; this is one reason cells stay small, or fold and flatten their surfaces.
claims.source: Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell (Garland Science), discussion of cell size and surface-to-volume; Campbell Biology (Pearson), 'Why are cells so small?' (surface-to-volume ratio, microvilli).

claims.text: Any shape scaled up evenly loses surface per volume in proportion to its size (surface scales as length^2, volume as length^3).
claims.source: Scaling every length by k multiplies area by k^2 and volume by k^3, so the ratio is divided by k.

claims.text: The cube cell and its units are made up; the shade on the stage shows surface per unit of inside relative to the width-1 cell.

recall.question: A round cell doubles its diameter. What happens to its surface per unit of volume?
recall.why: Surface grows 4 times and volume 8 times, so surface per volume halves (for a sphere it is 6 / diameter).
